plan.topic: Tirzepatide and semaglutide in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and obesity: an evergreen deep-dive on the randomized trials (SUMMIT for tirzepatide; STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM for semaglutide), with the Cedars-Sinai release (Oct 13) and the new JCEM tirzepatide meta-analysis as the hook
plan.angle: Evergreen SUMMIT decoder, hooked on SUMMIT itself (not news). Title: 'Did Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Help Heart Failure With Obesity (HFpEF)? What SUMMIT Found'. Segments 1–4 as planned, with every SUMMIT number (absolute event rates per arm, HR with CI, KCCQ change, analysed n, median follow-up) copied from the NEJM 2024 paper. STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM each get their own population and timeframe, labelled 'separate trials, not head to head'. Segment 5: 'What's next': (a) a confirmed 2026 meta-analysis with its real journal (e.g. Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice 2026, PubMed 42442557), described as pooled trial data; and (b) optionally the Cedars-Sinai European Heart Journal study (Oct 13, 2026), described ONLY as 'an early animal study in rats and minipigs, not a human result'. Do not mention its low doses and do not imply any human dosing. Segment 6: GI side effects with placebo rates. Segment 7: 'As of Oct 2026, tirzepatide is not FDA-approved to treat heart failure. Lilly withdrew its heart-failure application in 2025 after FDA asked for more data. It is approved for chronic weight management and obstructive sleep apnea.' Segment 8: cardiologist/prescriber questions, label contraindications. No dosing, switching or stopping advice. Close with 'talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you'.
plan.working_title: Does Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Help Heart Failure? What the SUMMIT Trial Found
plan.why:
Named-drug trial decoders are our proven long-form winner. The topic rests on well-documented NEJM randomized trials, so it can pass the fact-check in depth, and it has a fresh Oct 13 hook. | fact-check: The core topic is sound and evergreen. SUMMIT (NEJM 2024, NCT04847557) is real and fits a long-form trial decoder. Three problems with the hook need fixing first.
(1) The CEDARS-SINAI OCT 13 WORK IS AN ANIMAL STUDY, NOT OBSERVATIONAL. The Newswise release dated Oct 13, 2026 (European Heart Journal) tested LOW-DOSE semaglutide in rats and minipigs with an HFpEF-like condition. It reports less heart stiffness, enlargement and scarring without much weight loss. Calling it 'observational work … linked to' is wrong. Its 'low doses' framing could also read as a microdosing nudge, which is a banned topic. It may appear only as preclinical animal research, with no low-dose emphasis and no human implication.
(2) THE 'NEW JCEM TIRZEPATIDE META-ANALYSIS' COULD NOT BE VERIFIED. The October 2026 JCEM issue shows no such paper. The 2026 tirzepatide meta-analyses I found are in Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice (PubMed 42442557, Sept 2026: MACE OR 0.87; all-cause mortality OR 0.84) and Endocrine Practice ('Tirzepatide Beyond Diabetes and Obesity', 17 RCTs, which reports HFpEF HR 0.62, i.e. SUMMIT). Neither is JCEM. Either name a confirmed paper with its real journal or drop it.
(3) STATUS: tirzepatide has NO heart-failure indication. Lilly withdrew its HFpEF application in May 2025 after FDA asked for another trial. The label (revised Aug 2026, per secondary sources) covers chronic weight management and obstructive sleep apnea. Say this plainly. Prescribing for HFpEF is off-label.
The title should name HFpEF + obesity, not 'heart failure' in general. SUMMIT says nothing about reduced-EF heart failure. Keep STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM separate and not head to head. Keep the population for each segment exact: SUMMIT included people with and without T2D.

package.description:
Did tirzepatide (Zepbound) help heart failure with obesity? In SUMMIT, yes on both main measures, mostly through fewer heart-failure events. Not FDA-approved for heart failure as of Oct 2026.

SUMMIT (NEJM, Lilly-funded, 731 adults with HFpEF and obesity, median about 2 years): CV death or worsening heart-failure event 9.9% on tirzepatide vs 15.3% on placebo (HR 0.62). Symptom scores 6.9 points better than placebo at 52 weeks. CV deaths 2.2% vs 1.4%, too few to call. 6.3% stopped for side effects, mainly gut-related, vs 1.4% on placebo.

Education only, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
1. Packer M, et al. NEJM 2025 (online Nov 2024). https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2410027
2. Kosiborod M, et al. Lancet 2024 (pooled HF trials). https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24)01643-X
3. Lilly withdrew tirzepatide's HF application, 2025. https://conscienhealth.org/2025/05/03/lilly-withdraws-tirzepatide-application-to-fda-for-heart-failure/

script.working_title: Did Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Help Heart Failure With Obesity (HFpEF)? What SUMMIT Found
script.hook_pattern: Open loop plus stakes and specificity. The first line asks the title question, and absolute event rates answer it within about 15 seconds. Then the video opens a loop, "one number went the other way", which pays off in the cardiovascular-death section near the end.

scenes.narration: Did tirzepatide, sold as Zepbound and Mounjaro, help people with heart failure and obesity? In a trial called SUMMIT, the short answer is yes, on both of its main measures.
scenes.retention_device: Title question asked in the first line and answered within 10 seconds

scenes.narration: Over a median of about two years, 9.9% of people on tirzepatide had a worsening heart-failure event or died of cardiovascular causes, versus 15.3% on placebo.

visual.stat_label: HF event or CV death, ~2 years

scenes.retention_device: Concrete proof point with both arms

scenes.narration: But one number in that same paper went the other way. By the end of this video, you'll know exactly what it is, and why the trial was too small to call it either way.
scenes.on_screen_text: One number went the other way
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop planted (paid off in 'The number that went the other way')

scenes.narration: Here's the plan: what this type of heart failure is, what SUMMIT tested, the results in real numbers, how two semaglutide trials compare, the side effects, and the questions to bring to your cardiologist.
One thing up front: as of October 2026, tirzepatide is not FDA-approved to treat heart failure. We'll get to why.
scenes.retention_device: Second open loop (why it isn't approved)

scenes.narration: Heart failure is a scary name, but it doesn't mean your heart has stopped. It means your heart can't keep up with what your body needs.
Doctors sort it by ejection fraction: the share of blood your main pumping chamber pushes out with each beat.
In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, or HFpEF, that number is 50% or higher. The squeeze looks normal. The trouble is filling.
scenes.retention_device: Counterintuitive twist (normal pump, still heart failure)

scenes.narration: Picture a balloon made of thick, stiff rubber. The heart muscle doesn't relax and fill easily, so pressure can back up toward the lungs.

visual.stock_query: stiff rubber balloon hard to inflate

scenes.narration: That's why people with HFpEF often feel breathless, tired, and swollen in the ankles or legs, especially when they move.
Here's why this matters for GLP-1 medicines: many people with HFpEF also live with obesity, and researchers describe an obesity-related form where extra body fat and inflammation seem to add strain.
scenes.retention_device: Connects the topic to the GLP-1 viewer

scenes.narration: So researchers asked a bold question. If extra body fat is part of the problem, could a medicine that targets it ease the heart failure too?
scenes.on_screen_text: Treat the weight, help the heart?
scenes.retention_device: Question that sets up the next section

scenes.narration: SUMMIT was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial funded by Eli Lilly, which makes tirzepatide. It was published in the New England Journal of Medicine.
731 adults were randomized: 364 to weekly tirzepatide injections and 367 to placebo injections.
To join, people needed heart failure with an ejection fraction of 50% or more, a BMI of 30 or more, symptoms that limited their daily activity, and other signs of heart strain set by the trial.
scenes.retention_device: Exact population (so viewers can see if it applies to them)

scenes.narration: SUMMIT included people with and without type 2 diabetes. Remember that, because the semaglutide trials split those groups apart.
scenes.retention_device: Mini open loop (pays off in the semaglutide section)

scenes.narration: It was double-blind: neither participants nor their doctors knew who got the real drug. Median follow-up was 104 weeks, about two years.
There were two main questions. One: did fewer people die of cardiovascular causes or have a worsening heart-failure event? Two: did people feel better at one year?

items: CV death or worsening HF event

scenes.narration: A worsening heart-failure event meant a hospital stay, an urgent visit needing IV treatment, or stepping up oral diuretic pills for worsening heart failure.
So, did it work? Let's take the hard outcome first.
The combined outcome, cardiovascular death or a worsening heart-failure event, happened to 36 people on tirzepatide, 9.9%. On placebo, it was 56 people, 15.3%.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the first main question

scenes.narration: That's a hazard ratio of 0.62, roughly a 38% lower risk over time. The 95% confidence interval ran from 0.41 to 0.95, so the result was statistically significant.
scenes.retention_device: Relative figure paired with the absolute rates

scenes.narration: In plain terms: across about two years, roughly 5 fewer people out of every 100 had one of these events.
Most of that came from heart-failure events. They happened to 29 people on tirzepatide, 8.0%, versus 52 on placebo, 14.2%. Hazard ratio 0.54.
And the death part of that combined outcome? Hold that thought. That's the number that went the other way, and we'll open it up near the end.
The second main question was about daily life, measured with the KCCQ, short for Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire.
Its summary score rates symptoms and physical limits from 0 to 100, and higher is better. Basically: how much is heart failure getting in your way?
At 52 weeks, scores rose by an average of 19.5 points on tirzepatide, versus 12.7 points on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the second main question

scenes.narration: That's a difference of 6.9 points in favor of tirzepatide, with a 95% confidence interval of 3.3 to 10.6.

Wait, why did the placebo group improve by almost 13 points? Possible reasons: closer check-ups and extra attention in a trial, expectations that shape how people rate symptoms, and people often enrolling when they feel at their worst. That's why the fair comparison is against placebo, not against zero.
scenes.retention_device: 'But here's where it gets weird' question

scenes.narration: Other measures moved the same way. Six-minute walk distance, body weight, and a blood marker of inflammation called C-reactive protein all improved more on tirzepatide.
So on paper, SUMMIT hit both targets. But why would a medicine known for weight loss change how a stiff heart behaves?
scenes.retention_device: But/therefore pivot into a new question

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide activates receptors for two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP, which help regulate appetite and blood sugar.

visual.stock_query: two keys unlocking gut hormone locks

scenes.narration: The SUMMIT investigators' idea was that less body fat and less inflammation could ease the strain on a stiff heart. But the trial wasn't built to prove which piece mattered most.

visual.stock_query: heart relieved of weight and fire

scenes.narration: A smaller heart-MRI substudy of SUMMIT offered a clue. Compared with placebo, tirzepatide reduced the mass of the heart's main pumping chamber and the fat tissue around the heart.
But tirzepatide isn't the only GLP-1 medicine tested here. Semaglutide, sold as Wegovy and Ozempic, had two trials of its own, and the fine print matters.

visual.stock_query: two cartoon pens side by side

scenes.narration: Quick warning before any numbers: these are separate trials, with different people and different main questions. They were never compared head to head, so you can't rank the drugs from them.
scenes.on_screen_text: Separate trials, not head to head

visual.myth: SUMMIT vs STEP ranks the drugs
visual.fact: Separate trials, not head to head

scenes.narration: STEP-HFpEF, published in 2023 and funded by Novo Nordisk, enrolled 529 adults with an ejection fraction of 45% or more, a BMI of 30 or more, and no diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'groups split apart' loop

scenes.narration: Over 52 weeks, KCCQ scores rose 16.6 points on semaglutide versus 8.7 on placebo, a difference of 7.8 points.
Body weight fell 13.3% on semaglutide versus 2.6% on placebo, and six-minute walk distance rose 21.5 meters versus 1.2 meters.
STEP-HFpEF DM, published in 2024 and also funded by Novo Nordisk, tested the same idea in 616 adults with type 2 diabetes, using the same ejection fraction and BMI cut-offs.
After 52 weeks, KCCQ scores rose 13.7 points versus 6.4 on placebo, a difference of 7.3. Body weight fell 9.8% versus 3.4%.

Here's the key difference. Both STEP trials lasted one year and focused on symptoms, physical function and weight. They weren't designed to show whether hospital stays or deaths went down. SUMMIT was designed with that combined outcome as a main goal.
So what happens when you pool several trials together? That's where the evidence is heading next.

In 2024, The Lancet published a pooled analysis of four semaglutide trials: SELECT, FLOW, STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM. It looked at participants who had heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction.

Across those combined trials, fewer people on semaglutide had cardiovascular death or a worsening heart-failure event than on placebo, about 31% lower risk. That again came mainly from fewer heart-failure events; the effect on cardiovascular death alone wasn't statistically significant.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the pooling loop, echoing the 'which outcome?' theme

scenes.narration: Pooling helps when single trials are small, but it has limits. These trials enrolled different people for different main questions, so it's supportive evidence, not the final word.
For tirzepatide, the honest summary is one positive randomized trial, SUMMIT, plus supporting heart-MRI data. Before any of that matters to you, though, there are trade-offs.
In SUMMIT, the side effects that led people to stop were mainly in the gut. The label's most common ones are familiar for this class: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation.
Adverse events, mainly gastrointestinal, led 6.3% of people to stop tirzepatide, compared with 1.4% who stopped placebo.
According to the label, gut side effects are reported more often while the dose is being increased. Your prescriber manages that process, not the internet.
With heart failure there's an extra wrinkle. The label warns that dehydration from vomiting or diarrhea can lead to kidney injury, and many people with heart failure take water pills.
So don't guess with fluids. If you've been told to limit fluids, stick to that plan, and call your care team early if you can't keep food or drinks down.
In the semaglutide trials, serious adverse events were actually less common on the drug: 13.3% versus 26.7% on placebo in STEP-HFpEF, and 17.7% versus 28.8% in STEP-HFpEF DM.
The label also warns about gallbladder problems, pancreatitis, and low blood sugar when used with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Ask which warning signs mean call right away.

items: Low blood sugar with insulin or sulfonylurea

scenes.narration: Okay. Time to open the loop from the very start: the number that went the other way.

scenes.section: The number that went the other way
scenes.narration: Cardiovascular deaths in SUMMIT: 8 people on tirzepatide, 2.2%, versus 5 people on placebo, 1.4%.

scenes.section: The number that went the other way
scenes.narration: That's a hazard ratio of 1.58, which looks worse for tirzepatide. But the 95% confidence interval runs from 0.52 all the way to 4.83.

scenes.section: The number that went the other way
scenes.narration: That range is enormous. It covers a big benefit, no difference, and a big harm. With just 13 deaths in total, the trial can't tell those apart.

scenes.section: The number that went the other way
scenes.narration: So this result doesn't show that tirzepatide raised cardiovascular deaths, and it doesn't show that it lowered them. SUMMIT was too small to answer that question.

visual.fact: Too few deaths to tell either way

scenes.section: The number that went the other way
scenes.narration: Here's the bigger lesson. The headline result, 9.9% versus 15.3%, came mostly from fewer heart-failure events, not fewer deaths. Whenever you hear 'heart benefit', ask: which outcome?

scenes.section: The number that went the other way
scenes.narration: And that's exactly the kind of question regulators weigh.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the 'why not approved' loop next

scenes.narration: As of October 2026, tirzepatide is not FDA-approved to treat heart failure. In May 2025, Lilly said it had withdrawn its heart-failure application after the FDA indicated another confirmatory trial would be needed.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the second open loop

scenes.narration: In the US, as of October 2026, tirzepatide as Zepbound is approved for chronic weight management, and for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. As Mounjaro, it's approved for type 2 diabetes, and since August 2026 to lower the risk of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes at high risk. None of these is a heart-failure approval.

items: Moderate to severe sleep apnea with obesity (Zepbound)
Lower heart attack/stroke risk in T2D at high risk (Mounjaro, Aug 2026)

scenes.narration: So if a doctor prescribes it to someone with HFpEF, it's for one of those approved uses, or it's off-label. Either way, that's a decision for you and your clinician.

These medicines also aren't right for everyone. The label says not to use tirzepatide if you or your family have a history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2, or if you've had a serious allergic reaction to it.

items: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer

scenes.narration: So what do you actually do with all of this? Here's a checklist for your next appointment.
Question one: what type of heart failure do I have, and what's my ejection fraction? SUMMIT only studied people at 50% or above, with a BMI of 30 or more, plus other signs of heart strain.
Question two: how would a GLP-1 medicine fit with my diuretics and other heart medicines, and who will keep an eye on my fluids and kidneys?
scenes.on_screen_text: Q2: Fit with my heart meds?

scenes.narration: Question three: do I have an approved reason to take it, such as weight management, sleep apnea, or type 2 diabetes, and will my insurance cover it?
Question four: which side effects mean I should call you, and which can wait until my next visit?

Question five: how do I protect my muscle while losing weight? Ask about protein, checking first if you have kidney disease, and about cardiac rehab or strength training. Start gently, and check in if exercise is new to you.
scenes.retention_device: Links to the channel's muscle theme

scenes.narration: Quick recap. SUMMIT: 731 adults with HFpEF and obesity, about two years. Combined events, 9.9% versus 15.3%. Symptom scores, 6.9 points better. Deaths: too few to call.
Semaglutide's STEP trials: better symptom scores and more weight loss at one year, in separate trials, not head to head with tirzepatide.

factcheck.summary:
This script is accurate and safe to publish. I checked the key numbers against independent sources, and the rest matched the published results I know well.

**SUMMIT (the tirzepatide trial):**
- I confirmed against ACC's trial summary: 364 vs 367 people randomized, about 2 years of follow-up, 36 vs 56 primary events, and HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.41–0.95).
- The other SUMMIT figures match the published NEJM results as I know them, but I couldn't open the paper itself. They are: 9.9% vs 15.3% for the primary outcome; heart-failure events 8.0% vs 14.2% (HR 0.54); cardiovascular death 2.2% vs 1.4% (HR 1.58, 95% CI 0.52–4.83); KCCQ score change +19.5 vs +12.7 (difference 6.9, 95% CI 3.3–10.6); and 6.3% vs 1.4% stopping because of side effects.

**Semaglutide trials:**
- I confirmed the 2024 Lancet pooled analysis: 3,743 people, HR 0.69 for the combined outcome, heart-failure events HR 0.59, and cardiovascular death alone not significant (HR 0.82).
- STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM: I didn't open these papers. Their figures (529 and 616 people; KCCQ 16.6 vs 8.7 and 13.7 vs 6.4; weight loss 13.3% vs 2.6% and 9.8% vs 3.4%; serious adverse events 13.3% vs 26.7% and 17.7% vs 28.8%) match the published results as I know them.

**Other checks:**
- The heart-MRI substudy is real (JACC 2025; Kramer and colleagues; 175 people scanned). It found tirzepatide reduced the main pumping chamber's mass and the fat around the heart.
- The Mounjaro cardiovascular approval was dated August 28, 2026, for adults with type 2 diabetes at high risk of major cardiovascular events.
- Lilly withdrew its heart-failure application in May 2025 after FDA said another confirmatory trial would be needed.

**Framing and safety:**
- The script handles the cardiovascular-death number well: it gives the wide confidence interval, says it is too uncertain to call either way, and asks "which outcome?".
- Relative figures are paired with absolute rates. Novo Nordisk and Lilly are named as funders. The script says the semaglutide and tirzepatide trials were never compared head to head. Regulatory status is dated "as of October 2026".
- The fluid caveat, kidney caveat on protein, start-gently note on exercise, label contraindications and the prescriber line are all present.

There are a few small wording fixes below.

issues.claim: Did tirzepatide... help people with heart failure and obesity?
issues.problem: SUMMIT only studied one type of heart failure: HFpEF, with an ejection fraction of 50% or more. The first line makes it sound like it covers heart failure in general.
issues.fix: Did tirzepatide, sold as Zepbound and Mounjaro, help people with obesity and a common type of heart failure called HFpEF? In a trial called SUMMIT, the short answer is yes, on both of its main measures.

issues.problem: This gives only a relative figure, with no hazard ratio and no absolute rates. Our rules say every relative figure sits next to an absolute rate.
issues.fix: Across those combined trials, about 3,700 people with this kind of heart failure, fewer people on semaglutide had cardiovascular death or a worsening heart-failure event than on placebo: a hazard ratio of 0.69, about 31% lower relative risk. That again came mainly from fewer heart-failure events; the effect on cardiovascular death alone wasn't statistically significant.

issues.claim: serious adverse events were actually less common on the drug
issues.problem: This is accurate, but it could read as if the drug protects against serious events in general. It was a safety finding from two one-year trials, not something the trials were designed to test.
issues.fix: In the one-year semaglutide trials, serious adverse events were actually less common on the drug than on placebo: 13.3% versus 26.7% in STEP-HFpEF, and 17.7% versus 28.8% in STEP-HFpEF DM. That's a safety readout, not a main goal of those trials.

issues.claim: ConscienHealth URL as source for Lilly's withdrawal
issues.problem: This is a secondary blog, and the page returned a 403 error when I tried to open it. The search snippet does support the claim. Lilly's own statement would be a better primary source.
issues.fix: Keep the ConscienHealth URL, or swap in Lilly's Q1 2025 earnings release from investor.lilly.com if the pipeline can resolve a direct URL. Keep the wording 'Lilly said'.

issues.problem: These are our own explanations, and no source is tagged, which is correct. They are hedged as 'possible', so they're acceptable. Just make sure no source tag gets added to this scene.
issues.fix: No change needed. Keep source_ids empty and keep the word 'Possible'.

thumbnail.reasoning:
All three use the same clean heart-mascot style and brand colors, so legibility is generally good, but they differ in focal clarity and fit to our proven patterns.

#0 "FEWER HEART EVENTS?" (versus): Two expressive heart faces (anxious/sweating vs. happy) with clear PLACEBO/TIRZEPATIDE labels give an instant, honest contrast that mirrors the title's question. This is the exact 'versus' shape that produced our only long-form breakout (EloraTZP, 275 views) and is a trial-outcome framing, not sensationalized — the question mark keeps it hedged. At phone size the two faces and VS are still crisp and the labels, while small, are short single words and readable. Single clear focal point (the contrasting faces) with strong emotional pull.

#1 "THE CATCH?" (mystery): The black silhouette heart with a giant question mark is a strong curiosity hook, but the sub-headline "Not FDA-approved for HF" is small, dense text that becomes nearly unreadable at phone/small size (a known QA pattern — text under ~40px). It also risks feeling like it's withholding/teasing rather than answering, which is a softer match to the title (which asks about heart failure benefit, not approval status) — slight curiosity-gap mismatch that could read as clickbait-adjacent on a sensitive medical topic.

#2 "FELT BETTER?" (before-after): Clear, legible, nice emotional arc (tired/sleepy heart to lively heart), but it answers a different question (quality of life/KCCQ) than the title asks (heart events), creating a mild mismatch between title and thumbnail promise — viewers searching for the heart-failure-events answer may feel the image doesn't match. Still legible and pleasant, but less targeted than #0.

Given legibility ≥7 for all, #0 offers the strongest combination of emotional contrast, a direct match to the title's actual question (events, not symptoms or approval status), adherence to our proven 'versus' format, and full legibility even at small sizes.

issues.claim: Did Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Help Heart Failure With Obesity?
issues.problem: SUMMIT only enrolled people with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (EF 50% or more). 'Heart failure' on its own is wider than the trial population. The description fixes this, but the title is where the population should be exact. Adding one abbreviation stays within the rule of at most one.
issues.fix: Did Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Help Heart Failure (HFpEF) With Obesity?

issues.problem: The thumbnail headline 'FEWER HEART-FAILURE EVENTS?' doesn't say which heart-failure population. The subtext has room to add it.

issues.claim: In SUMMIT, worsening heart-failure events fell (8.0% on tirzepatide vs 14.2% on placebo)
issues.problem: The trial population is missing, which breaks the 'state the trial population exactly, everywhere' rule. Also, 'fell' suggests a drop over time when this is a between-group comparison. The script says 'happened to'.
issues.fix: In SUMMIT (731 adults with HFpEF and obesity, about 2 years), worsening heart-failure events happened to 8.0% on tirzepatide vs 14.2% on placebo, but cardiovascular deaths went the other way: 2.2% vs 1.4%. With only 13 deaths in total (HR 1.58, 95% CI 0.52 to 4.83), the trial was too small to call it either way. Tirzepatide is not FDA-approved for heart failure as of Oct 2026. Save this for your next cardiology visit. This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
